title: Sitaphal, Fig and Smoky Charcoal: Indian Sweets and Regional Fruits Are Rewriting Ice Cream Menus
excerpt: Makers are reinterpreting mithai and regional fruit as scoops — Grameen Kulfi, Rose Gulkhand, jackfruit and tender coconut — without displacing the classics, says Iceberg Organic Ice Creams founder Suhas B Shetty.
body:
• Indian ice cream makers are reimagining regional fruits and traditional sweets as scoops, Hindustan Times reports, citing Iceberg Organic Ice Creams founder and CEO Suhas B Shetty.
  • Regional fruits gaining ground include mango, sitaphal and fig — including a fig-and-almond combination — alongside jackfruit and tender coconut.
  • Mithai-led flavours Shetty named include Grameen Kulfi, Creamy Malai, Kaju Kismis and Rose Gulkhand; the experimental edge includes a smoky charcoal made using burnt tender coconut shells.
  • The classics are not being replaced: butterscotch, chocolate and kulfi remain in demand. The shift, Shetty says, is expanding what ice cream can be, not displacing it.

The newest flavours in Indian ice cream are some of its oldest tastes. Makers are reinterpreting regional fruits and traditional sweets as scoops — not as novelties, but as the main line of experimentation, Hindustan Times reports.

"The shift is not about replacing classic flavours, but about expanding the definition of what ice cream can be."

— Suhas B Shetty, founder and CEO, Iceberg Organic Ice Creams

Shetty told the paper he is seeing a growing affinity for flavours that are both nostalgic and local. "Today's consumer is willing to experiment with something completely new, especially when there is an interesting ingredient or story behind it," he said. The appeal, he said, is familiarity combined with novelty: a recognisable taste in an unfamiliar form.

Regional fruit, by the scoop

Mango remains, in Shetty's words, "one of the strongest and most universally loved flavour profiles," while sitaphal and fig-based flavours are gaining attention among consumers moving beyond conventional options. Fig and almond is one combination he cited. Jackfruit and tender coconut are also finding their way into scoops.

At the experimental end sits smoky charcoal, which Shetty described as made using burnt tender coconut shells — a flavour built entirely from an ingredient most kitchens throw away. The pattern matches what brands such as NIC have built menus around: gajar halwa, gulab jamun and kesar pista scoops made with the actual dessert ingredients rather than flavouring alone, and seasonal jackfruit sold only while the fruit is in season.

Mithai, reinterpreted — not just frozen

On the sweets side, Shetty named Grameen Kulfi, Creamy Malai, Kaju Kismis and Rose Gulkhand among the traditional flavours being explored. "The idea is not to merely recreate a traditional dessert in frozen form, but to take familiar Indian taste memories and reinterpret them through different textures, creaminess, and combinations," he said.

The same logic is showing up across the premium segment: Frootrition's survey of mithai-fusion concepts notes paan, kesar-pista, Alphonso mango and traditional sweet flavours gaining attention in premium ice cream through the year, with a Diwali peak, and cites an IMARC projection, via Tetra Pak, of India's ice cream market growing about 11% a year to Rs 57,500 crore by 2033.

Who is driving it

Shetty pointed to two audiences discovering the flavours: Gen Z buyers, with social media encouraging experimentation, and older consumers drawn by nostalgia. The overlap is the commercial point — a sitaphal scoop is a discovery post for one generation and a childhood memory for the other, sold in the same tub.
